ap_chemistry-f01.title: Titration of a weak acid with a strong base

stimulus.description: A student titrates $20\text{ mL}$ of a $0.1\text{ M}$ solution of the weak monoprotic acid $\mathrm{CH_{3}COOH}$ ($K_a=1.80\times10^{-5}$ at $25^\circ\text{C}$) with $0.2\text{ M}$ NaOH. Indicators available: methyl orange (pH 3.1–4.4); bromocresol green (pH 3.8–5.4); methyl red (pH 4.4–6.2); bromothymol blue (pH 6.0–7.6); phenolphthalein (pH 8.2–10.0); alizarin yellow R (pH 10.1–12.0).

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Write the equilibrium expression and calculate the pH of the acid solution before any NaOH is added.
parts.model_answer: $K_a=[\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{A^-}]/[\mathrm{HA}]$; with $x=[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$, $x^2/(0.1-x)=K_a$ gives $x=0.00133\text{ M}$ and $\mathrm{pH}=2.88$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes $K_a=[\mathrm{H_3O^+}][\mathrm{A^-}]/[\mathrm{HA}]$ or the equivalent ICE-table expression
common_errors: writes Kw instead of Ka

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $[\mathrm{H_3O^+}]$ (about 0.0013 M)
common_errors: assumes complete dissociation

rubric_rows.criterion: Reports the pH (about 2.88)
common_errors: gives the pOH

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the volume of NaOH, in mL, required to reach the equivalence point.
parts.model_answer: moles of acid $0.002$; $V=10.0\text{ mL}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the moles of acid (0.002 mol)
common_errors: uses mL without converting to L

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the equivalence volume (about 10.0 mL) with units
common_errors: uses the acid volume as the base volume

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the pH of the solution at the half-equivalence point, and explain how the result is related to the acid.
parts.model_answer: At half-equivalence $[\mathrm{HA}]=[\mathrm{A^-}]$, so $\mathrm{pH}=\mathrm{p}K_a=4.74$.

rubric_rows.criterion: States pH equals $\mathrm{p}K_a$ (4.74) at half-equivalence
common_errors: gives the pH at equivalence

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains that $[\mathrm{HA}]=[\mathrm{A^-}]$ there, so $\log([\mathrm{A^-}]/[\mathrm{HA}])=0$ in the Henderson–Hasselbalch equation
common_errors: says the acid is neutralized completely

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Select the most appropriate indicator for this titration from the list and justify your choice.
parts.model_answer: phenolphthalein: the pH at equivalence is about 8.8, inside its color-change range, because the conjugate base of a weak acid makes the equivalence-point solution basic.

rubric_rows.criterion: Selects phenolphthalein
common_errors: selects the indicator closest to pH 7

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with the equivalence-point pH (about 8.8) lying within the indicator range because the solution contains the weak conjugate base
common_errors: says equivalence is at pH 7

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: The student repeats the titration with the same volume of acid at double the concentration. Does the volume of NaOH needed to reach equivalence change? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Yes, it doubles, because the moles of acid double and the moles of base needed are in a 1:1 ratio.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the equivalence volume doubles because the moles of acid double (1:1 ratio)
common_errors: says it does not change because Ka is unchanged

ap_chemistry-f02.title: Free energy, equilibrium and a galvanic cell

stimulus.description: For a reaction at $298\text{ K}$: $\Delta H^\circ=-57\text{ kJ/mol}_{rxn}$ and $\Delta S^\circ=-188\text{ J/(mol}_{rxn}\cdot\text{K)}$ (both independent of temperature). Part (d) concerns a different system: a galvanic cell built from $\mathrm{Pb}$/$\mathrm{Pb^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{Ag}$/$\mathrm{Ag^{+}}$ half-cells connected by a wire and a salt bridge, with standard reduction potentials $-0.13\text{ V}$ and $+0.80\text{ V}$ respectively. Each half-cell contains the metal electrode in a solution of its ions under standard conditions.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Calculate $\Delta G^\circ$, in kJ/mol, for the reaction at $298\text{ K}$.
parts.model_answer: $\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ=-1.0\text{ kJ/mol}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses $\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ$ with entropy converted to kJ
common_errors: omits the unit conversion

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $\Delta G^\circ$ (about -1.0 kJ/mol) with units
common_errors: uses a Celsius temperature

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Determine the temperature at which the reaction changes between thermodynamically favorable and unfavorable, and state whether the reaction is favorable above or below that temperature. Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: $\Delta G^\circ=0$ at $T=\Delta H^\circ/\Delta S^\circ=303\text{ K}$; the reaction is favorable below this temperature because $\Delta S^\circ$ is negative.

rubric_rows.criterion: Sets $\Delta G^\circ=0$ and solves $T=\Delta H^\circ/\Delta S^\circ$
common_errors: divides ΔS by ΔH

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the temperature (about 303 K)
common_errors: leaves ΔH in kJ

rubric_rows.criterion: States the reaction is favorable below that temperature, citing the sign of $\Delta S^\circ$ in $\Delta G^\circ=\Delta H^\circ-T\Delta S^\circ$
common_errors: links favorability to the sign of ΔH alone

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the equilibrium constant, $K$, at $298\text{ K}$.
parts.model_answer: $K=e^{-\Delta G^\circ/RT}\approx 1.5$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses $\Delta G^\circ=-RT\ln K$ with R in J/(mol·K) and ΔG° in joules
common_errors: uses kJ with R in J

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $K$ (about 1.5)
common_errors: omits the negative sign

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: Sketch a diagram of the galvanic cell described in the stimulus. Label the anode, the cathode and the direction of electron flow in the external wire, and calculate the standard cell potential.
parts.model_answer: The anode is the half-cell with the less positive reduction potential (Pb2+/Pb); $E^\circ_{cell}=0.93\text{ V}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws the two half-cells with a wire and salt bridge, labels the Pb2+/Pb half-cell as the anode (more negative reduction potential, where oxidation occurs) and the other as the cathode, and shows electrons flowing from the anode through the wire to the cathode
common_errors: identifies the more positive half-cell as the anode

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $E^\circ_{cell}=0.93\text{ V}$ (cathode minus anode)
common_errors: adds the potentials

parts.label: E
parts.prompt: Calculate $\Delta G^\circ$ for the cell reaction, if 2 moles of electrons are transferred per mole of reaction, and state what the sign of the result indicates.
parts.model_answer: $\Delta G^\circ=-nFE^\circ=-179\text{ kJ/mol}$; the negative value shows the cell reaction is thermodynamically favorable.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $\Delta G^\circ$ (about -179 kJ/mol) and states that the negative sign means favorable
common_errors: omits the number of electrons

ap_chemistry-f03.title: Concentration–time data and the order of a reaction

stimulus.description: Concentration of A in the reaction A → products at 310 K

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Determine the order of the reaction with respect to A. Describe the graph you would plot to test your answer and explain how the graph supports your conclusion.
parts.model_answer: The reaction is first order. A graph of ln[A] versus t gives a straight line, while the graphs of the other two linearized forms curve.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the reaction is first order in A
common_errors: picks the order whose plot is curved

rubric_rows.criterion: Names the axes of the graph to plot: ln[A] versus t
common_errors: plots [A] versus t only

rubric_rows.criterion: Explains that the points of this graph fall on a straight line, whereas the other linearized plots are curved
common_errors: cites only that [A] decreases with time

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Using the graph, determine the rate constant, $k$. Give the value as a decimal number (not in scientific notation) with units.
parts.model_answer: $k=|\text{slope}|\approx 0.0090\text{ s}^{-1}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Obtains the slope magnitude of the linear graph (about 0.0090 in the units of the graph)
common_errors: uses a slope from the curved graph

rubric_rows.criterion: States $k\approx 0.0090$ as the magnitude of the slope
common_errors: gives the slope with the wrong sign

rubric_rows.criterion: Gives the units of $k$ as s⁻¹
common_errors: gives units of a second-order constant for a first-order reaction

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Calculate the half-life of the reaction for the initial concentration in the table.

rubric_rows.criterion: Uses the half-life relation for a first-order reaction: 0.693/k
common_errors: uses the second-order relation

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates the half-life (about 77 s)
common_errors: divides instead of multiplying

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The experiment is repeated at a higher temperature. Predict whether $k$ increases, decreases, or stays the same, and justify your answer using the collision model.
parts.model_answer: $k$ increases: at the higher temperature a larger fraction of collisions has energy at least equal to the activation energy.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that $k$ increases
common_errors: states k decreases because particles collide more often

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with a larger fraction of collisions that exceed the activation energy (and more frequent collisions)
common_errors: says the activation energy decreases

ap_chemistry-f04.title: Photoelectron spectrum of an element

stimulus.description: Photoelectron spectrum of a neutral atom of element X. The height of each peak is proportional to the number of electrons in that subshell. Peaks (binding energy in MJ/mol, relative number of electrons): (178, 2); (15.1, 2); (11.5, 6); (1.46, 2); (0.79, 2).

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Identify element X and write its complete ground-state electron configuration.
parts.model_answer: The peak heights show 2 + 2 + 6 + 2 + 2 = 14 electrons, so X is Si: 1s$^{2}$ 2s$^{2}$ 2p$^{6}$ 3s$^{2}$ 3p$^{2}$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies X as Si (the peak heights sum to 14 electrons) with the configuration 1s$^{2}$ 2s$^{2}$ 2p$^{6}$ 3s$^{2}$ 3p$^{2}$
common_errors: counts the number of peaks instead of the number of electrons

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Explain, using Coulomb's law, why the peak with the highest binding energy corresponds to the electrons in the 1s subshell.
parts.model_answer: The 1s electrons are closest to the nucleus, so the Coulombic attraction between them and the nucleus is greatest (Coulomb's law: the force is larger at a smaller distance), and the most energy is needed to remove them.

rubric_rows.criterion: Cites the smaller distance of the 1s electrons from the nucleus and the resulting larger Coulombic attraction
common_errors: says the 1s electrons are shielded the most

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: The element that follows X in the periodic table is P, which has one more proton. Is the binding energy of the valence-electron peak of P higher or lower than that of X? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Higher: P has one more proton, and its extra electron enters the same subshell, which adds little shielding, so the effective nuclear charge is larger and the Coulombic attraction for the valence electrons is greater.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that the valence peak of P is at a higher binding energy than that of X
common_errors: says the peak of the next element is at a lower binding energy

rubric_rows.criterion: Justifies with the greater nuclear charge acting on electrons in the same subshell with little added shielding (Coulomb's law)
common_errors: says the electrons are farther from the nucleus

ap_chemistry-f06.title: Lewis structure, geometry and boiling points

stimulus.description: Consider the molecule $\mathrm{XeF_{4}}$ and the two compounds $\mathrm{CH_{3}OH}$ (32 g/mol, normal boiling point 338 K) and $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$ (30.1 g/mol, normal boiling point 185 K).

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Draw a Lewis electron-dot diagram of $\mathrm{XeF_{4}}$ that shows all of its valence electrons.
parts.model_answer: XeF4 has 36 valence electrons in total: the diagram shows 4 bonds from the central atom to the other atoms, 2 lone pairs on the central atom, and the remaining lone pairs on the outer atoms.

rubric_rows.criterion: Draws a Lewis diagram that accounts for all 36 valence electrons, with 4 bonded atoms and 2 lone pairs on the central atom
common_errors: omits the lone pairs on the central atom

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Use your diagram to identify the molecular geometry of $\mathrm{XeF_{4}}$ and the approximate bond angle.
parts.model_answer: square planar; bond angle 90° (six electron domains (four bonding pairs and two lone pairs) are arranged octahedrally with the lone pairs on opposite sides, giving a square planar shape).

rubric_rows.criterion: States square planar geometry and a bond angle of 90°
common_errors: reports the electron-domain geometry instead of the molecular geometry

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: Is the $\mathrm{XeF_{4}}$ molecule polar or nonpolar? Justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: Nonpolar: the bond dipoles cancel because the shape is symmetric.

rubric_rows.criterion: States nonpolar and links it to the symmetric arrangement, in which the bond dipoles cancel
common_errors: decides by the polarity of the bonds alone

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The data in the stimulus show that $\mathrm{CH_{3}OH}$ has a higher boiling point than $\mathrm{C_{2}H_{6}}$ even though it has a similar molar mass. Explain this difference in terms of intermolecular forces.
parts.model_answer: CH3OH molecules form hydrogen bonds with one another, which are stronger than the attractions between C2H6 molecules, so more energy is needed to separate the molecules of CH3OH.

rubric_rows.criterion: Identifies hydrogen bonding between CH3OH molecules as stronger than the attractions between C2H6 molecules, which raises the boiling point
common_errors: says covalent bonds within the molecules break when the liquid boils

ap_chemistry-f07.title: Equilibrium expression, Q versus K and disturbances

stimulus.description: At a certain temperature the equilibrium $\mathrm{A}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\,\mathrm{B}(g)$ has $K_c=0.5$ and is endothermic. A cylinder with a movable piston initially contains $[\mathrm{A}]=0.5\text{ M}$ and $[\mathrm{B}]=0.1\text{ M}$ at this temperature.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Write the equilibrium-constant expression, $K_c$, for the reaction.
parts.model_answer: $K_c=[\mathrm{B}]^2/[\mathrm{A}]$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes $[\mathrm{B}]^2/[\mathrm{A}]$ (products over reactant, with the coefficient as an exponent)
common_errors: omits the exponent 2

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the reaction quotient, $Q$, for the initial mixture and determine the direction in which the reaction proceeds.
parts.model_answer: $Q=0.1^2/0.5=0.02$, which is less than $K_c=0.5$, so the reaction proceeds toward the products.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $Q\approx 0.02$ and states the direction as forward by comparing Q with K
common_errors: reverses the comparison of Q and K

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: After the system reaches equilibrium, the piston is moved so that the volume of the cylinder is doubled at constant temperature. Predict the direction of the shift and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The system shifts toward the products: the expansion lowers the concentrations, $Q$ becomes less than $K_c$, and the side with more moles of gas (two moles of B instead of one of A) is favored at lower pressure.

rubric_rows.criterion: States the shift toward the products and justifies it with Q becoming less than K (or the favored side having more moles of gas)
common_errors: says K changes with volume

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The temperature is then increased. Does the value of $K_c$ increase or decrease? Justify your answer using the sign of the enthalpy change.
parts.model_answer: $K_c$ increases: for an endothermic reaction heat acts as a reactant, so raising the temperature favors the products.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that $K_c$ increases because heat behaves as a reactant in an endothermic reaction
common_errors: says K does not depend on temperature

key_conditions.condition: the reaction is gas-phase in a cylinder with a movable piston

verification.independent_path: Q computed exactly and compared with K by the sign of ln(Q/K); the volume-change direction follows from recomputing Q after the change

parts.label: A
accepted_answers: $K_c=[\mathrm{B}]^2/[\mathrm{A}]$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes $[\mathrm{B}]^2/[\mathrm{A}]$ (products over reactant, with the coefficient as an exponent)

parts.label: B
accepted_answers: $Q=0.1^2/0.5=0.02$, which is less than $K_c=0.5$, so the reaction proceeds toward the products.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $Q\approx 0.02$ and states the direction as forward by comparing Q with K

parts.label: C
accepted_answers: The system shifts toward the products: the expansion lowers the concentrations, $Q$ becomes less than $K_c$, and the side with more moles of gas (two moles of B instead of one of A) is favored at lower pressure.

rubric_rows.criterion: States the shift toward the products and justifies it with Q becoming less than K (or the favored side having more moles of gas)

parts.label: D
accepted_answers: $K_c$ increases: for an endothermic reaction heat acts as a reactant, so raising the temperature favors the products.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that $K_c$ increases because heat behaves as a reactant in an endothermic reaction

ap_chemistry-f07.title: Equilibrium expression, Q versus K and disturbances

stimulus.description: At a certain temperature the equilibrium $\mathrm{A}(g) \rightleftharpoons 2\,\mathrm{B}(g)$ has $K_c=2$ and is endothermic. A cylinder with a movable piston initially contains $[\mathrm{A}]=0.5\text{ M}$ and $[\mathrm{B}]=0.3\text{ M}$ at this temperature.

parts.label: A
parts.prompt: Write the equilibrium-constant expression, $K_c$, for the reaction.
parts.model_answer: $K_c=[\mathrm{B}]^2/[\mathrm{A}]$.

rubric_rows.criterion: Writes $[\mathrm{B}]^2/[\mathrm{A}]$ (products over reactant, with the coefficient as an exponent)
common_errors: omits the exponent 2

parts.label: B
parts.prompt: Calculate the reaction quotient, $Q$, for the initial mixture and determine the direction in which the reaction proceeds.
parts.model_answer: $Q=0.3^2/0.5=0.18$, which is less than $K_c=2$, so the reaction proceeds toward the products.

rubric_rows.criterion: Calculates $Q\approx 0.18$ and states the direction as forward by comparing Q with K
common_errors: reverses the comparison of Q and K

parts.label: C
parts.prompt: After the system reaches equilibrium, the piston is moved so that the volume of the cylinder is doubled at constant temperature. Predict the direction of the shift and justify your answer.
parts.model_answer: The system shifts toward the products: the expansion lowers the concentrations, $Q$ becomes less than $K_c$, and the side with more moles of gas (two moles of B instead of one of A) is favored at lower pressure.

rubric_rows.criterion: States the shift toward the products and justifies it with Q becoming less than K (or the favored side having more moles of gas)
common_errors: says K changes with volume

parts.label: D
parts.prompt: The temperature is then increased. Does the value of $K_c$ increase or decrease? Justify your answer using the sign of the enthalpy change.
parts.model_answer: $K_c$ increases: for an endothermic reaction heat acts as a reactant, so raising the temperature favors the products.

rubric_rows.criterion: States that $K_c$ increases because heat behaves as a reactant in an endothermic reaction
common_errors: says K does not depend on temperature
